claims.text: THE QUALIFICATION, WHICH TRAVELS WITH THE ARTICLE AND IS ROUTINELY DROPPED. The description is what Lazar told the reporter, not an employment record. Stanton Friedman, who obtained the Los Alamos telephone directory page carrying Lazar's name, records that the page 'clearly states that it includes employees of the DOE and outside contractor, Kirk Meyer'. A Los Alamos colleague interviewed on tape by Mark Farmer on 25 May 1996 said Lazar 'was a contractor' under 'Kirk Mayer' and that he 'claimed to be' a physicist. Tom Mahood's 2018 conclusion is that Lazar worked as an electronic technician for Kirk-Mayer and that the Monitor article misrepresented his position on the basis of what he told the reporter.

claims.text: It is also the date peg for the Edward Teller anecdote, and it creates a discrepancy rather than resolving one. Tom Mahood's 2018 retrospective puts the article on 27 June 1982 with Teller lecturing at Los Alamos the following day, and calls the timing an 'amazing display of totally fucked synchronicity'. Lazar's own 1991 narration places the newspaper story and the Teller speech on the same day. The newspaper's date is fixed, so both cannot be right.

claims.text: THE SECOND-BEST FINDING IN THIS CLUSTER: TWO PEOPLE REACH THE SAME COUNTER-EXPLANATION BY UNRELATED ROUTES. Tom Mahood, a physics graduate who spent years on the documentary record, concludes in his 2018 retrospective that there is 'nothing at Papoose Lake' and that S-4 actually refers to a radar facility at the Tonopah Test Range. Separately, T.D. Barnes, a former CIA and NASA engineer who worked at Groom Lake, says the real Site 4 is a remote radar site north of the main facility that held captured Soviet equipment, that this and not an underground base is what Lazar referred to, and that a named retired Area 51 security chief confirmed to him that Lazar appears on no manifest. Neither route depends on the other: one is documentary and civilian, the other is recollection by a former range engineer. Shared conclusions from a shared method are not corroboration; these two do not share a method.

On the Los Alamos question he concludes that Lazar worked as an electronic technician for the contractor Kirk-Mayer rather than as a staff physicist, that the phone-directory listing reflects that contractor relationship, and that the Monitor article's description followed what Lazar told the reporter. He also accepts that the W-2 could be legitimate, representing a brief stint at Groom, while insisting 'it doesn't mean saucers exist at Papoose'.

claims.text: His 2018 retrospective concludes that there is 'nothing at Papoose Lake', that S-4 actually refers to a radar facility at the Tonopah Test Range, and that Lazar constructed the alien-craft narrative as a cover after security caught him bringing friends to watch classified tests in April 1989. claims.text: THE COUNTER-DESIGNATOR, AND THIS IS A DISPUTE RATHER THAN A LINK. Tom Mahood's 2018 retrospective states that there is nothing at Papoose Lake and that the designator 'S-4' actually refers to a radar facility at the Tonopah Test Range. T.D. Barnes, a former CIA and NASA engineer at Groom Lake, reaches the same conclusion by an unrelated route, describing the real Site 4 as a remote radar site holding captured Soviet equipment. Neither is claiming that Lazar's described facility is at Tonopah; both are claiming that the designator he used belongs somewhere else entirely.
